albums.take: "That We Can Play" feels like getting dropped somewhere between Blue Planet and an old PlayStation. I loved the whimsy of the opening and darker ending, even if the middle lost some of that magic.
albums.review:
I had never heard of Games, and I honestly had no idea what to expect from a recommendation from Nick K.

But as soon as “Strawberry Skies” came on, I knew listening to this album anywhere other than a dimly lit room with the lamps on for vibes would not do it justice.

I loved the introduction. It brought back memories of playing Nicolas Jaar mixes while watching Planet Earth in college. The trickling water, the muted voice, and the xylophone-like rhythm transported me somewhere else almost immediately.

“Midi Drift” kept that feeling going, drifting me off into synthwave land with a little chiptune mixed in. I had a blast with that one.

“Shadows in Bloom” had some great moments too, but this is where the album started losing me a little. The beginning had this whimsy and uniqueness to it where all the clashing sounds and sudden switch-ups somehow flowed perfectly. As it went on, though, everything started feeling busier. There were so many noises happening at once that some of the songs began to blur together.

It was not bad. It just did not feel as effortless or distinct as those first few tracks.

After such a strong start, I started losing the vision of what the rest of the album was trying to do.

Then I heard the familiar sound of the PlayStation booting up, followed by that huge crescendo, and suddenly I was back in.

The closing Gatekeeper remix of “Strawberry Skies” takes the song somewhere completely different from the original. It is darker, heavier, and lowkey feels like it belongs in Far Cry: Blood Dragon, which I absolutely mean as a compliment.

Overall, I enjoyed this album. I could easily see myself putting it on in the background while debugging some coding issue or designing a user interface. And if I ever find myself watching Planet Earth again, or, even more fittingly, Blue Planet, I know what I’m putting on.

albums.take: "Hypnotize" mixes chugging guitars and absurd repetition with sharp political commentary. I wanted more Serj, but grew to appreciate Daron's vocals, and the title track remained my favorite.
albums.review:
I had only heard what was on the radio and seen what was played on MTV, so I'm glad my babe asked me to listen to this album.

What I didn't expect was how much guitarist Daron sings. I wanted to hear more Serj at first, but I came to appreciate the way the two trade vocals.

I hate to say it, but my favorite song was the one I already knew: "Hypnotize." It is such a great song, with an intro that puts you into a trance through the strumming of the guitar and the climb of the notes. The repetition of "I'm just sitting in my car waiting for my girl" really drives home the strength of propaganda and the complacency many of us have toward modern issues.

"Tentative" and "Holy Mountains" were standouts as well.

There is a lot of repetition in the lyrics, especially on "U-Fig" and "Vicinity of Obscenity." "Banana terracotta terracotta pie" repeated over and over makes me feel absurd while listening to it. But I enjoyed the journey of hearing those lyrics shouted over the chugging guitar.

I feel entitled and absurd as I sit here sipping a salted coconut latte with oat milk and coconut water while reflecting on this album, especially as the songs make me think more about what's happening in the world. But that's the point of this album, right?

albums.take: Thirteen years stuck on one song and the album around it is half great. "Hell and Back" still sounds like a fight I won, "Say Please" ambushes you at track 11, the middle blurs. Album is worth a shot.
albums.review:
Discover Weekly handed me back a song I had not thought about in years, and a couple seconds in I was 23 again.

I was wrapping up college and had just come out of a year of straight F's. My medical leave was not approved, I did not withdraw in time, and the transcript said what it said. I was devastated and I was angry. Then Hell and Back came on.

The song made me feel heard. I had been to hell and back and I was still standing: about to graduate, a year of astronomy research behind me, just home from an observing trip to Lick Observatory. Family matters had cost me a lot mentally and academically. I would put that song on at SW Rec and lift heavy ass weights. 

Then I did what you do with a song like that. I played it to death. Never listening to the rest of the album. 

I got around to listening to the rest today. 

The first twenty minutes are bangers. The title track plays like a movie about teenage heartbreak, and the lyrics are not complicated or deep, but I am not sure they should be for that kind of love. The ending is exactly as soft as it needs to be.

The other surprise came late. Say Please is the second to last track and I fell for those  haunting chords immediately and for the cry of "ooooo, oh oh". I had it on at the gym all day today.

The rest does not hold up the same way. Too many songs blur into each other, and an hour later I could not tell you which was which. On the front half alone this album is a 4. Whole, The Other Side is a strong 3.5 out of 5.
